From its beginnings, the GIRSU project recognized the need to acknowledge and integrate the waste pickers who worked at the open-air landfill under highly precarious labor and social conditions. Until then, most of these workers relied on informal waste collection for their livelihoods, without institutional recognition or adequate working conditions. In this context, the implementation of the GIRSU represented a significant shift in how waste management was conceived in the region, incorporating recycling as part of a public service and recognizing the fundamental role of waste pickers within the system. This perspective allowed progress toward formalizing employment, promoting social inclusion, and improving working conditions for a historically marginalized sector.
The COTRANVI Workers' Cooperative was already established when the project began and had 12 members. However, the growth of the recovery, sorting, and marketing of recyclable materials, driven by the GIRSU program, led to a significant expansion of the organization, which reached approximately 80 members by the end of 2023.
This growth translated into substantial improvements in workers' conditions, both in terms of infrastructure and safety, as well as in terms of the stability of the business and the income earned. It also strengthened collective organizing processes and consolidated the cooperative's role as a central player in the public policy for integrated waste management.
However, from 2024 onwards, difficulties began to emerge that affected the overall functioning of the system. The reduction of support programs, the economic difficulties facing the recycling sector, and the drop in demand for recovered materials negatively impacted the activity. As a result, some of the progress made in terms of social and labor inclusion was jeopardized.
Currently, the GIRSU Separation Plant continues to be the main workspace for the members of the cooperative, who maintain the tasks of recovery and classification of recyclable materials in a significantly more complex context than that recorded during the years of greatest expansion of the system.

Initiative: Botellas de amor
Answer in English:
Although the initiative has been successful in mobilizing citizens and recovering large quantities of flexible plastic waste, several limitations became evident during its implementation. One of the main challenges relates to logistics. As the collection network expanded across multiple provinces, the transportation of materials over long distances to centralized processing facilities became increasingly complex and costly. Because flexible plastic packaging has a low density and relatively low economic value, the environmental and economic costs associated with collection, storage, and transportation can become significant, particularly when collection points are located far from processing plants.

A second limitation is related to the quality of the recovered material. The initiative collects a mixture of flexible and multilayer packaging composed of different polymers that cannot be easily separated. While this approach provides a practical solution for materials that would otherwise be discarded, it does not enable closed-loop recycling. Instead, the mixed plastics are transformed into plastic lumber products. As a result, the final material generally has lower quality and fewer potential applications than products manufactured from sorted, single-polymer recycled plastics.

If the initiative were to be redesigned, a more decentralized processing system could be considered to reduce transportation distances and associated costs. In addition, greater emphasis could be placed on improving material segregation at the source and promoting packaging designs that facilitate recycling. Such measures could increase material quality, improve resource efficiency, and reduce dependence on long-distance logistics.

The main lesson learned is that social participation and stakeholder coordination can successfully recover plastic waste streams that are typically excluded from conventional recycling systems. However, long-term sustainability requires not only citizen engagement but also careful consideration of logistics, transportation impacts, material quality, and the availability of local processing infrastructure. In other words, recovering waste is not sufficient on its own; the entire value chain must be environmentally, technically, and economically sustainable.
